newsitem.title: UK: Kirkham trusts may sell up to 22 pct of DFS.
newsitem.headline: Kirkham trusts may sell up to 22 pct of DFS.

text.p: The founder of fast-growing British upholstered furniture retailer DFS Furniture, Sir Graham Kirkham, said on Wednesday that his children and some family trusts were considering cutting their shareholding in the company and could sell "a significant proportion" of their 22 percent holding in the company.

"Subject to market conditions and subject to price they intend to make a significant proportion off their 22 percent holding in DFS available to institutional and other investors," the company said in a statement. Kirkham added he would not be selling any of my own personal shareholding.

The executive chairman said the move reflected his children's wishes, and the fact that they have no involvement at all in the running of the company, whereas in Kirkham's own case, he confirmed "without reservation that my commitment to the company remains as strong as it has ever been".
Kirkham, who built up DFS from an operation based around a single factory into a nationwide store network, is well-known as a wealthy supporter of the ruling Conservative party.

The company was floated in 1993. Its latest results for the full year to July 27, also announced on Wednesday, showed pretax profit up nearly 19 percent to 31.1 million stg, on turnover up 27 percent to nearly 185 million stg.
Kirkham described the results as "record-breaking", saying they showed excellent growth while the firm expanded at "an unprecedented pace with eight store openings".

"Our proven track record and these excellent results speak for themselves, so understandably my confidence in our ability to continue to break records and to achieve long-term targets for sustained, quality profit growth has never been higher", he said in the results report.

As well as paying a final dividend of 6.9p per share, to add to an earlier interim dividend of 3.1p, for a year-on-year rise of 20.5 percent, DFS also proposed a special dividend of 10p at a cost of 10.4 million stg.
This would be "the most equitable course" to return surplus cash to shareholders, the board had decided, following a review of its future income and ancticipated capital expenditure.
The board added it believed that DFS cash position "exceeds the requirements of the business for the forseeable future".
